utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer. Anyone else behind the column? All right. Any preliminaries? The matter that you wish to deal with, we'll deal with it as soon as we conclude the other issue that we had -- we were dealing with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I'm in no rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Neither are we. Any other preliminaries? None. All right. So I suggest we go into closed session. And please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your indulgence, could I come closer to my clients so I can explain why the blinds have been raised so he understands what's going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. I would even go further than that. Let's have a break of five minutes, and you can speak to him in private in the room outside. So we'll have a five-minute break or as long as you need, Madam. If you need more than five minutes, we will be here waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, ten minutes is what I need, if I could have ten minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. For the time being, if the cameras could not focus on the witness's face, please. So we'll have a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.24 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome back, Madam Isailovic. Have you had an opportunity to advise your client, explain to him what the situation is now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I was able to explain him briefly what was the nature of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Mr. Jokic, what's going to happen now is I'm going to explain to you the procedure that we intend to follow, and I'm also going to explain to you what is provided for in our rules, and then I will proceed with our conclusion for today, which will be followed by a written order in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed, Mr. Jokic, I take it that you are still determined not to testify. I just need a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not feel fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So according to Rule 77 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Tribunal, in the exercise of its inherent powers, may hold in contempt those who knowingly and wilfully interfere with the administration of justice, including any person who, being a witness before a Chamber, contumaciously refuses or fails to answer a question. You have repeatedly refused to testify, and in these circumstances, the rules provide in (C) of the same Rule 77 that when a Chamber has reason to believe that a person may be in contempt of a Tribunal, the Trial Chamber can -- has the following options: It can direct the Prosecutor to investigate the matter with a view to the preparation and submission of an indictment for contempt, following which, were the Prosecutor in the view of the Chamber has a conflict of interest with respect to the relevant conduct, direct the registrar to appoint an amicus curiae to investigate the matter and to report back to the Chamber whether there are sufficient grounds for instigating contempt proceedings, or ultimately to initiate proceedings itself. We have reason to believe that you may be in contempt of the Tribunal and our decision is to opt for the last of these options, to choose the last of these options, namely to initiate proceedings ourselves. Paragraph (D) of Rule 77 further provides that in such cases, when the Trial Chamber decides to initiate proceedings itself, it can issue an order instead of an indictment, and either direct amicus curiae to prosecute the matter or prosecute the matter itself. We have decided to prosecute the matter ourselves. We need to advise you that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in parts 4 and 8 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings under this rule. Last but not least, because this you will to have deal with in consultation with the registrar and your counsel for the time being, any person indicted or charged for contempt shall, if that person satisfies the criteria for determination of indigence established by the registrar, be assigned council pursuant to Rule 45. Madam Isailovic has been assigned to you, I take it, for the purpose of the subpoena and not for the purpose of contempt so following our order, which we'll issue in the course of the day, you will need to initiate negotiations with the registrar for assignment of counsel for the purpose of the contempt proceedings if you satisfy the criteria laid down in the directives that are applicable. Our consideration, our decision, is that on the face of it, by refusing to testify, you have contravened Rule 77(A) on the face of it, and in terms of Rule 77(C), we have reason -- we have reason to believe you to be in contempt of the Tribunal. We have, as I told you, decided in the particular circumstances that it is appropriate to initiate proceedings in terms of Rule 77(C)(iii), to be such -- such proceedings to be prosecuted by the Chamber itself in terms of Rule 77(D)(ii). The charge against you will be formulated in the course of the day and it will be issued in a written order and you will be served with a copy of it in due course. I've got nothing to add for the time being. Next time we meet, Mr. Jokic, will mark the beginning of the contempt proceedings against you. I think the witness can leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Isailovic, I apologise to you for having addressed you as Madam Ismailovic -- or I pronounced your surname wrongly on a couple of occasions. My apologies to you. I am in the habit of doing that. Thank you. Thank you for your assistance, Madam Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from here. Mr. McCloskey, I stand to be corrected because we were involved in discussions on this matter and in preparing for this morning's sitting, and I haven't had a chance to verify after yesterday evening. Two days ago, I asked you to be kind enough to respond to the Beara team's confidential motion. I don't intend to go into details as to its merit. I just mention that. And I had directed your attention that we needed your response by yesterday evening. I again stand to be corrected. I haven't -- by yesterday evening, I hadn't come across your response. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was filed yesterday afternoon, around 5.00, 5.30 p.m., somewhere around there, Your Honours, electronically filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me and my apologies to you. We'll see it and -- it still hasn't arrived. Have you been notified of it, Mr. Ostojic or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, we have not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that disposes of that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We could send out courtesy copies right away. When we filed it yesterday afternoon, we explained that it was a deadline filing and I will try to get that out right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The next thing, yesterday we had Mr. Josse wishing to address the Chamber for about ten minutes on the Prosecution motion to add 18 documents to the 65 ter list in relation to the -- or to Witness number 30. I think we can mention his name freely, no? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure there won't be an application for protective measures for this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine so. In any case, there have already been decisions in relation to his testimony, so I wouldn't expect protective measures but I just wanted to make double sure. Before I give you the floor, did any of the other Defence team file any response? Because again once more we haven't come across any filings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware and I've discussed it with some of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Josse could you kindly deal with this issue and you have as much time as you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me begin by making it clear that, in fact, so far as the motion is concerned in relation to these 18 exhibits, there is no opposition. And it may be that what I'm about to say in summary, the Trial Chamber would like put into writing. However, bearing in mind the shortness of time, I thought the Trial Chamber might want me to include this in effect in relation to the exhibit issue because it's similar. On the 30th of October, very helpfully, my learned friend Mr. Thayer provided the parties with the proofing notes of General Smith, whom he saw on, I think the 22nd of October, and then had telephone conversations with on the 27th and the 30th of October. One particular entry on that proofing note is a real concern to us, and in effect we want to move that the Prosecution be prevented from asking the general any questions in relation to that area. I have briefly spoken to Mr. Thayer and he tells me that he proposes to ask some questions so far as that area is concerned. Your Honour, perhaps the best thing is if I ask that the proofing notes be put on the ELMO and the Trial Chamber will have in front of them the -- one aspect of these notes that I'm concerned about. I'm -- as the Court knows from previous submissions that I've made, I always take the view that if I'm going to deal with matters like this, the Court needs to know exactly what the matter in hand is, if the submission succeeds then no doubt you'll put it out of your mind. If it fails, you're going to hear about it any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me, however, consult with my colleagues because this becomes necessary each time it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Josse. We agree completely with your submission. Let's have it disposable. If there is an extra copy that you can make available, Mr. Thayer, then Mr. Josse can keep his.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got several, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Up, please. Up. Up. That's fine, thank you. About the middle of the page, the Court will see, and I will read this out, it says, "He," obviously referring to General Smith, "Recalls that on the day he left Zepa for the last time, he encountered General Gvero at a check-point at the outskirts of Zepa. When they got out of their vehicles, Gvero told him that Mladic was heading to another front and that Gvero was now in charge of the Zepa operation. He next saw Gvero in Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st of July." This in our submission is a significant and important allegation. It's not an allegation that has been made by any witness hitherto. Let me be clear, Your Honour, the fact that Smith and Gvero met in Mrkonjic Grad on the 31st of July was certainly known to us and that's not the part we are quibbling about. It's the sentences immediately before that one. To the best of our knowledge, not only has this allegation not been made by any witness before, but it's not been made by any witness before, but it's not been made in any form at all in this case. It's certainly not in the indictment. It's not in the pre-trial brief, nor was it in my learned friend's opening statement. Indeed, in essence, the pre-trial brief at paragraph 182 makes it clear that the Prosecution case was that it was General Tolimir who was in charge of events at Zepa. Our objections are twofold. First of all legal and technical. So far as the legal and technical basis is concerned, we place particular reliance on the fact that this allegation was not alleged in the indictment. We submit that if such an allegation is to be made, it needs to be made by way of a specific averment to that effect in the indictment and that because that has not been done, the Prosecution should be debarred from leading this evidence. But aside from that legal and technical objection, perhaps more importantly, on this occasion, we can show real prejudice if the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecution to lead this evidence. Assuming that we are right and that this is a new allegation and not one that's previously been made, we submit that had we been made aware of it at an earlier stage, we would undoubtedly have conducted our case in a different fashion. It's a subject that we would have explored with a significant number of witnesses who have already given evidence in this case. Namely, whether our client was present in and around Zepa at the time as alleged in these proofing notes by General Smith. In particular, and this list is not exclusive, we would have explored it with Witnesses Dibb, Joseph, Savcic, Milovanovic, Palic, Torlak, and Skrbic. I choose them in particular because none of them were protected. And perhaps others. But certainly those in particular. And, Your Honour, the failure of the Prosecution to alert us to this particular significant, important allegation prior to the 30th of October prejudices us in a real and significant way for reasons that I hope are obvious. In addition to that, and this is a subsidiary point, we contend that this allegation might have some further legal impact inasmuch as it might trigger requirements under Rule 67(A)(1)(a), in relation to a defence of alibi. I'm not going to go into this in a great deal of detail because that particular rule, which I'm not going to read out, uses the word "alleged crime." And the question of course is whether the allegation that my client was in Zepa at the time means that he was present at the site of an alleged crime. It's not an altogether easy issue and it's not one -- I don't know whether it's been decided in this particular Tribunal. But it certainly means that it raises the spectre of us perhaps having to deal with that at this particular stage and of course, it will also mean that we will have to expand our investigations to look for potential witnesses who could counter the allegation as made in these proofing notes. So, Your Honour, we submit that this is a profound and important allegation and for the reasons that I've set out in this brief oral submission, the Prosecution shouldn't be allowed to lead it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning to Your Honours, good morning to everyone. The information at issue here was provided for the first time to the Prosecution in this proofing session that's referred to in these notes. This is entirely new information to the Prosecution that General Smith brought forward in the discussion of some of these documents concerning generals -- General Gvero's involvement in the Zepa events. It was something that he just flat out mentioned and frankly it took me by surprise because I'd never heard this information myself, nor seen it anywhere. But he has a very clear, distinct recollection of these events and we notified Defence counsel. The context, I think, in terms of any surprise or prejudice needs to be understood with respect to General Gvero's involvement as charged in the JCE forcibly to remove the civilian population from Zepa. We do not understand the Court to have required the Prosecution to plead every piece of evidence tying each of these accused to the JCEs in which they were charged. There are numerous pieces of evidence which the Court has already heard that we allege tie General Gvero to that JCE forcibly to remove the Muslim population from Zepa. Some examples, Your Honours, 65 ter 1320, the phone conversation intercept between General Smith's military assistant, Colonel Baxter, in which he arranges through General Gvero a meeting to discuss with General Smith the resolution of the Zepa situation. In that conversation General Gvero is clearly well informed and reveals that he's obviously close to Mladic. That conversation, in fact, results in a meeting on the 25th, memorialised in 65 ter 191 -- actually in 65 ter 2747 in which there is a meeting held between Generals Smith, Mladic, and Gvero to discuss the events in Zepa. We have 65 ter 191 in which General Tolimir communicates to Generals Miletic or Gvero as stated on the communication regarding the agreement that had been reached on the 24th between Mr. Torlak and General Mladic, and in which he notes the obstacle of the fate of the Srebrenica men to an overall agreement. And we also have on that same day the 25th of July, 65 ter 182, where General Mladic issues an order regarding restricting access to Zepa which is directed to General Gvero's sector. And we also have another meeting on the 31st of July, again held to resolve the issue of Zepa and the fate of the military-aged men in Mrkonjic Grad which we have referred to already again attended by Generals Smith, Mladic, and Gvero. All of this evidence has been known to Defence counsel, I would say respectfully, for years, 18 months in some case to two years. This has been pled in our pre-trial brief, at page 60. These specific meetings and documents are specifically referred to. They are specifically discussed in Rick Butler's Main Staff command responsibility report at pages 25 to 26 and the foot notes therein. This new information provided by General Smith is perfectly consistent with this hands-on, active role played by General Gvero in these events. To that extent, this is no change in theory, it is not a surprise. If anything it is perfectly consistent with what the government's theory has been -- with the Prosecution's -- I time travelled there for a moment, Your Honours. Forgive me. And it's interesting that my friend referred to alibi. I was thinking during his address that we had an order from the Court directing parties to file notices of alibi or alibi and we had known. We understand the positions of some of Defence counsel that in a JCE alibi is an inchoate concept. We disagree. But Defence counsel has chosen its strategy. This new information is not inconsistent with the Prosecution's evidence, which has been long known to Defence counsel. And there is no reason for General Smith not to be able to testify about it, to be challenged upon it, and if Defence counsel has to undertake some additional investigation, or based on the testimony as it comes in, if Defence counsel feels that it can make a showing that additional questioning of other witnesses on this limited topic is something that is necessary, then we can address that issue. But it's not a reason to foreclose this testimony from General Smith, which is relevant and, again, fits in perfectly consistently with what the evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, all I've got to say is it may be consistent but it is completely new. We have chosen a particular way of defending this case in the light of the allegations hitherto made, and we can categorically say that we would have chosen a different course had this allegation been known to us when this trial started. And on that basis, we submit that General Gvero has been prejudiced. It's also all very well my learned friend saying that we can, on showing good cause, ask for these various witnesses to be brought back here. It's an awful lot of witnesses, all of whom could undoubtedly have given germane evidence on the point in question. And finally, my learned friend makes light of the fact that this has not specifically been averred in the indictment. We submit that this is a matter of such significance that it really needed to be averred in the indictment because otherwise it makes a nonsense of the particularisation that the Prosecution have chosen to embark upon in this indictment in relation to each of the accused. Because this is such a significant allegation, for it to raise its head, it needs to be in the indictment, we submit. But Your Honour, I do emphasise that though I place reliance on that legal and technical basis perhaps the stronger ground here is the prejudice to the way this Defence has been run hitherto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Josse. We'll consider your submissions in due course and we'll come back to you but obviously you don't expect a decision now. So otherwise, as regards the admission or not the admission, sorry, the inclusion of these documents in the 65 ter list for the purpose of General Smith's testimony, there seems to be agreement, so your motion is granted in the absence of any objections, Mr. Thayer. When I say your motion, it's the Prosecution's motion, not yours. Third thing, yesterday -- Madam Nikolic, I'm going to address you. Yesterday -- I'm going to read out to you briefly the exchange of submissions and comments that went on between you and I yesterday, Madam Nikolic. At a certain point in time, I told you, you said, "As I asked the Chamber today on page 43 of the transcript, the request of my Defence team was for the Trial Chamber to allow to exceed ten pages, it wouldn't be more than 15 pages. The interpreters didn't follow that, that's one thing. Another thing, on behalf of the Defence teams who jointly wrote a submission regarding about the testimony, we would like the Trial Chamber to exceed, that is, to extend the deadline for our objection until 9 November 2007, that is an extension of only three days which would enable us to prepare an adequate submission. "Page 82, submission, not objection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 17270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The thing is, at the end of the sitting, our attention -- our attention was drawn to whether, from the transcript, from what you had said, it was clear as to which submission or filing you were referring to. And the reason for this is the following: That if you intended or you were referring to the appeal from our decision in Butler, okay, I'm referring obviously to Butler, then unfortunately, I have to go back on what I granted you on behalf of the Trial Chamber yesterday because it's not within our competence to grant any extensions of time or of length of -- I think you would agree with me that those have to be addressed to the Appeals Chamber, but as it was, I don't think we were on the same wave length yesterday. I apologise to you and to everybody for not catching up exactly what you meant. But again I take back whatever we granted yesterday. Please be advised that that needs to be addressed to the Appeals Chamber, and I hope that is clear enough to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours, good day to my colleagues. I thank you for this clarification and I immediately noticed my own error after I read the transcript when I returned to the office, so I'm grateful for this clarification of your position. And I expect, as far as your approval for additional pages for our submission, has remained the same. So if I may consider that as something that's approved and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, submission, which submission? For the --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we have a problem with the translation. I'm going to be very brief. The submission that has to do with strike from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That stands. That stands, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we move to the next witness, ladies and gentlemen, you will recall that sometime back, Mr. McCloskey voicing also the concerns of the Defence teams, briefly addressed the Trial Chamber on whether you would be receiving any information, any directives, in relation to the Rule 98 bis proceedings and should there be a decision to proceed with the case, then also in relation to the preparation of the Defence cases, particularly the time frame which will be required for the filing of all 65 ter documents. I want to put your mind at rest that we had not slept over this or shelved it or put it in deep freeze. We have been actively thinking and discussing about all this, and we haven't come back to you before now for the very simple reason that the situation was shifting. We got an impression that there were only 16 witnesses left and that the case would be over more or less at end of November. That lasted very short time. We are now talking of the first week of February, considering the short break that we are giving you to round up your preparations for another important witness. But we have been actively discussing this, as I said, and we believe that the time now calls for the matter to be dealt with and be determined because we do have a view of the end of the tunnel which we can work with. We have got ideas, of course, because we have been discussing, as I said, but we wouldn't like to reach any decisions before giving you, both of you, the opportunity to be heard. We'll hear what you have to say, what your wishes or what you believe are your requirements in this regard, and together, then, we'll -- that will help us come to a complete time frame which we will communicate to you once we have reached a decision. For this purpose, we had in mind inviting you to make oral submissions, the sooner the better. It all depends actually on the witness schedule that we have at the moment, and how long you would -- you expect to take, how much time you require, to make your submissions to the Trial Chamber. Of course, we will be discussing with you a few issues as well. So I would suggest we choose together a sitting when we will deal with these issues, and as I said, the sooner the better. Now, we have a situation arising, Mr. McCloskey, whereby instead of hearing the testimony of the guy who left the courtroom earlier on, we will be having contempt proceedings. That might take longer or shorter. I don't know. But it certainly requires an interval of time for the preparation of the case, on his part in particular, and for the registrar to assign him counsel and whatever. So I don't know how you intend to fill in that space because there will be a space. We do have a witness now who is, I suppose, ready to testify. We can start with him today. But I don't know what the situation you have to enlighten us on this. I don't know what the situation is going to be as soon as this witness finishes his testimony, whether, in other words, you have another witness -- we do have one on Monday, for sure. We have one on Monday for sure but I don't know what the position is going to be tomorrow, and I don't know what the position is going to be the rest of the -- of next week. So if you can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Thayer has all the details on those, and although I wanted to just, as you brought up the 98 bis issue and oral submissions, I just would throw out one idea that I will discuss with counsel but that, as we know the new law on 98 bis was designed to make things shorter and briefer, and I'm not sure it had us in mind when it said that. I mean, seven Defence counsel and the Prosecution, because as you can imagine, that will -- that could take two weeks, if we just had a few hours each for each person we have, as you know, a large indictment. You may want to consider, and I'll discuss it, that this be done in writing and that any oral submissions be very limited to what the Court wants to hear. It's not hard for the Prosecution to put our side in writing but we're willing to of course go oral as well, but we might save sometime if we went back to the old system but that's just an idea, food for thought, and on the more practical matters I will turn it over to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, it may well be that when we amended the rule way back in 2004, we were not -- we did not have in view the -- this particular case, but the rule as it stands now specifically refers or uses the words "After hearing the oral submissions of the parties," and that was in lieu of what we had before, which provided for written submissions. But in any case, we'll allow you the opportunity to discuss amongst yourselves, and then to provide us with a date when we could have this constructive exchange of views here, which would enable us to come to a decision within the shortest possible time. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have the next witness available. The Defence has estimated about four hours of cross for him. It's likely to be shorter, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's likely to be shorter given the nature of things. In either case we've advised our friends that the gap filler is available, as always, on the issue of the Drina Corps collection. So if necessary, he will be available, suited up, tomorrow to fill out the day. As for the remainder of the schedule, it seems to me that it's intact as of today. We have General Smith ready to go Monday morning. We've estimated five days for him, direct and cross. He is available for that additional day. After the break we'll see if we need it. I think the schedule is still solid after that as well. So with respect to the witness that was here earlier today, depending on what happens, we'll find the time to insert him down the line, if that becomes necessary. But I think we can proceed on the schedule that we've gotten. We'll just have to play it by the ear until then. If I may, I didn't want to interrupt Mr. President the points you were making just now. I did have a thought that occurred to me on my friends' issue with the proofing note, a light bulb went off in my head. I haven't had my coffee this morning so I'm a little slower than even usual, but if I could just address this one thought that came to me on that issue. We faced a similar situation with respect to General Gvero's involvement in the Zepa JCE with Colonel Trivic, who you may recall, commander of the Romanija -- 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade testified. As happens, he said something to me in a proofing session which was new information, he in fact placed General Gvero at one of the Zepa forward command posts during these -- this time in question. That information was communicated to my friends in the proofing note, and they were able to deal with it. It was brand new information, information that no party had heard before, just like this information coming from General Smith. We have no control over that information or when we get it. But when we heard it we disclosed it and my friends were able to deal with it. So I don't see why at this point we have to take this extreme step of excluding the information when they have been able to deal with such information in the past. Placing General Gvero in the heart of these matters, as we've pled he has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still don't have an answer as to when we are going to have an opportunity to hear submissions on what I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that you are going to have mutual discussions and then you come forward with a proposition for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, and I don't think Mr. Thayer is suggesting otherwise, of course in cross-examination Colonel Trivic resiled from that position in effect or certainly said that he couldn't be certain about it, and said that he might well have be confusing what he was saying about our client being at the IKM with seeing him at the Zivanovic leaving party. So the position is rather different, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now, 25 minutes, and we start immediately with the next witness afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why isn't the witness present?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, the witness had indicated that he would prefer the extension of the protective measures that were granted to him previously. I had indicated that to Defence counsel in both my proofing note and in a follow-up e-mail that I would make an oral application to the Court. As you know, he was on stand by yesterday. I proofed him on Monday. So that's the reason why he's not here just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The protective measures that were extended in the previous matter were just a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None. So that is granted. We will be told, I think, what number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It would be PW-169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: PW-169, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's the protective measure that is being granted. I think we can bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are soon going to proceed with your testimony, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before we do so, I want to tell you two things. First, that we have just finished discussing your wish expressed to the Office of the Prosecutor to have the same protective measure that you enjoyed when you testified previously in another case restated today, and the Prosecution made the request. No Defence team opposed it. And therefore, we have granted you the protective measure of being able to testify under a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me finish. With a pseudonym instead of with using your real name. But before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be telling us the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of this solemn declaration. You've seen it before. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I thank you so much, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will start, now start hearing your testimony. Mr. Vanderpuye will go first for the Prosecution. He will then be followed by the Defence teams. We don't expect your testimony to finish today, although we'll do our best. In any case, it won't last beyond tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again good morning to you. Good morning to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. May I have 65 ter 2932 please shown to the witness? Sir, please look at that document. Don't tell us what's on it, and can you tell us if that's -- if you're the person that's named on it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you show it to one or more of the Defence teams who wish to see it. Yes. Do you wish to go into private session for the first part, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness I just wanted to direct your attention to the events of the 11th of July 1995. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in relation to that day, did you decide to take some action with respect to the safety of yourself and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: On that day, I was gathering hay in the meadow for my cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: In the early evening, perhaps about two hours before night fall, we saw this column from other villages, people walking, and then people called out to me from the other fields around, they said, "Let's go home, Srebrenica has fallen." So I got home and at home I found my neighbours at this particular point, and with packed bags and they said, "What are you waiting for? Do you see that everybody is on the move?" And they said somebody came from the civilian protection, and they said that the old and infirm should go to the UNPROFOR base at Potocari; whereas military-age men should go through the forest. So I, together with my family, left. I took a few things and took the horse and set out towards Potocari. I arrived in Potocari, it was already night-time. They told us that we were going to the battery factory where the UNPROFOR base is. When we got close to the factory, there were already lots of people around, other factories. So what was all of this about? They said that that we couldn't go to the battery factory, but that we were supposed to stay up there. So we stopped there by this first factory on the left-hand side when entering Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a moment. About what time was it that you got this information about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: It could have been around 9.00. I'm not sure. It could have been around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just finish my question. I know that sometimes a take a little long to ask them but -- what was it that you were doing -- about what time was it that you received this information that Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Say around 5.00, when they told me that Srebrenica had fallen, and that we should go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long after you received this information did you set out to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, maybe -- well, say it was like half an hour, because this field where I was gathering hay was about five minutes away from my home. It wasn't further away than that. So I left my home around half an hour later, say it was around 5.30, say up to 6.00, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you leave with your family or other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: With my family, and then I caught up with other people, so we walked in this column, with people we did not know, from my area, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Without telling us their names, with whom from your family did you leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I left with my wife, my daughter-in-law, one of my grand daughters, and my daughter. So there was five of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how is it -- how did you actually go from your town to Potocari? How did you travel there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I had a horse, so I rode the horse. We were travelling across the hills where it's closer, and they were with me on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is there any particular reason why you went on horse while they went on foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, I was unfit. In 1982, I injured my leg and it's hard for me to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About how long did it take you to get from your town to Potocari after you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: About three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And around what time did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: In Potocari, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: It could have been around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Dark, dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did you go initially when you got to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: To the compound where the Sacmara factory is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us where that is in relation to the UNPROFOR compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Before the UNPROFOR compound, say about 500 metres away, I'm not sure but it's about 500 metres before that. That's where this factory was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you directed to go to that particular building, or did you just decide to go there on your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, we went to where there was enough room to sit down. We found some room around that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to what was going on at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: We spent the night there at that compound, in the parking lot there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that with several other people or with just your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of people. This compound was full. It all got full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened the morning of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Some people went down there to the gate of the UNPROFOR base to ask what would happen to us then. Then they would come back from there, and they said that there would be some transportation for Tuzla, that we should wait. They didn't know when or who would transport us, but they said that they were told that there would be some kind of transportation. So that is how we saw Serb soldiers getting close to these factories around there. Some of them setting hay on fire. So we already saw them, those who were on the edge saw the Serb soldiers getting closer. On that afternoon, I cannot remember exactly what time it was, perhaps it was around 2.00, the first convoy arrived, and they said some vehicles have arrived to take people. I went around the column and, in front of the compound of Ekspres Strela, and then by the slaughterhouse and then I got to the road. There were roadblocks, barricades, there. UNPROFOR put this rope there. And then behind the rope, they were standing there, so they saw -- we saw this road narrowing down, the road that we would be taking to get to the buses. So I saw these barricades and up to the buses, these camouflage -- soldiers in camouflage uniform, they were all lined up in this column of people walking by.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't want to interrupt my colleague, but I believe that I heard from the witness that those guys were holding each other's hand right in front of this rope and I don't see this in transcript. So maybe he can clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose the witness has heard what Mr. Lazarevic has just commented or remarked. Do you agree with Mr. Lazarevic, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If could you answer Mr. President's question, sir? My colleague has put to you that part of your testimony isn't in the record here, referring to soldiers holding hands.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: It was UNPROFOR. It wasn't the Serb soldiers. On the road. Serb soldiers were down the road, lined up down the road, by the battery factory to the trucks and the buses and the Serb soldiers were not holding hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just describe the uniforms that you saw these Serb soldiers wear, as best as you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: They had multi-coloured uniforms, dark green and even a bit darker than that. Multi-coloured uniforms. I cannot tell you exactly but dark green and even darker than that. Really dark green, multi-coloured. They are not white. They are even darker green.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say multi-coloured, do you mean a type of camouflage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Camouflage, camouflage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how many soldiers, if you can estimate, Serb soldiers, did you see lined down this road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, I cannot -- well, say four or five metres, one next to the other, but there would be four or five metres between them and then 120 metres or so or even more than that, up to the buses. Maybe even 50 metres. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. Perhaps it was about ten soldiers, about ten, for sure, who were lined up by the canal and then there were other soldiers just standing around.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you at any point receive some direction with respect to boarding these buses or the transportation that had been provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Nothing, because I didn't even get close to those buses. As soon as I passed by that roadblock a Serb soldier took me by the shoulder and told me to go left to the other end of the road and to stand there, and I saw our elderly men standing there already. They had been singled out. And they said, "You just go and stand there. That's what they told me to do too." So I just stood there and they were still separating these men and separating them and separating them, and when they singled out this group, there were about five or six soldiers around us, they said, now go up there to that house, it was a new house that hadn't been built completely. It just had a roof on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were asked to step over to one side of the road and stand there, were you there with your family at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No. No. I asked that soldier why are you separating us? Why are you separating me from my family? And he said, "You have time to go but let the women and children go earlier on. You go left." And that's how I left. My family went towards the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see other men being separated from their families as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how many of you were told to stand over to one side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Perhaps about 20 of us were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to see what happened to your family once that soldier told you to step over to one side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, I saw that they went towards the buses and then I couldn't see anything any more, what was going on around the buses. I couldn't see then. I couldn't know. They did reach the bus, though. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After the group of about 20 of you had gathered, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Then they told us that we should not stand there, that we should go up to that house that hadn't been completely built yet. We went to that house and they followed us and we entered that house. We were there on the ground floor. And then we sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The soldiers who directed you to go to the house? Were they wearing the same uniforms as the ones you had seen lining up the road, lining down the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were they -- were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes, everyone of them had an automatic rifle. I didn't see any other weapons, just automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About how far from the road was this house that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, perhaps it was about 50 metres, maybe even more than that. Well, as far as I can tell, it's around 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you escorted there by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you arrived at the house, tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Then they were guarding that house, the soldiers were standing in front of the house, some would threaten us about what they would do to us that night, some took out knives saying that they would slit our throats, and then someone said that that one should move away, that he had nothing to do with us, that he shouldn't touch us. They were not all behaving the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what the conditions were like in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: The house didn't have a floor. It just had brick or block constructed walls. There was a ground floor, there were no windows or doors. We went in. There was a large room, and we sat down in that large room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you given any water and any food during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time that you arrived at this house, were there other men inside, other --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No. We arrived first at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And after you arrived at the house, were there other men that came afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. Groups were arriving of about 20 people, and then they were sitting in front of the house. There was no more room in the house. When the basement was filled or the ground floor was filled, they were sitting in front of the house then. These were all men. I remember we were asking the soldiers why we were being separated. They said we don't know anything why you are being separated. We don't know anything about what would happen. And then, after a while, again, we asked and said, "Do you know why we are being separated now?" And then one said General Mladic is coming now, so you can ask him why you're being separated. We don't know. . Then the same route that we took from the road, an officer came, bare headed in a camouflage uniform. He had rank insignia, and he was escorted by three or four soldiers. He entered through the door of the house, and he said, "Good day, neighbours." He said, "Did you see what Alija has done to you? Were you thinking that the NATO pact would save you? But we are not afraid of the NATO pact. We were bombed by them but they couldn't do anything to us. Now, Srebrenica has fallen and Gorazde will fall, and Bihac will fall, then Sarajevo." So he went on enumerating, and then he said Tuzla will be the last to fall. Why didn't you go to Fikret Abdic? Why did you stick with Alija? Then I said I'm not interested neither in Fikret Abdic nor in Alija. What I want to know is why we are being separated from our families. And he said, we have Serbs -- 180 Serbs who are captured in Tuzla, so we need 180 of you in order to effect an exchange because your people won't let them go. And I'm going to exchange you, he said. Then he went back, the same way that he came to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: By your estimate, as best as you can, about how many men were in this house and around the house during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Later, I can confirm that when we got to the buses, there were two buses, they were full. All of us fitted into those two buses. We didn't do any counting. The two buses were packed. People were standing up in the aisle. Not everyone was able to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And of the men that were in and around the house during the time that you were there, were there any young men with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us what kind of men were with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: They were all of my age, and at the same level of disability, and there were even some men who were older and more disabled than I. Some of them even had walking sticks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About how long after this conversation, or I should say this speech that you've described, how long after that did you actually go to the buses and leave that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour to an hour and a half. I'm not sure but that's about how much time passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how much time had passed from the time that you first arrived at the house until the time that you boarded the buses, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: We spent four hours in the house definitely, maybe even a bit longer, but I'm not sure, but definitely about four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how was it that you were taken from the house or you went from the house to the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: When it just got dark, the sunset, but you could still see quite well, they told us, well, the buses are here, stand up now and go out. You can go to the road in front of our soldiers. The buses are waiting for you. Those who were outside stood up first and then they left. Then we left the house last, and I could see soldiers lined up at a distance of ten metres, one from the other, and they told us, well, go in front of our soldiers. And I could see a column in front of Serbian soldiers going past and they were just saying, hurry up, hurry up. Then we turned a little bit to the right. We made a semi-circle across the fields. We got to the battery factory, and I could see they were entering the last bus, the men. By the time I crossed over, the last bus was full and then they were going into the first bus. I got into the first bus. General Mladic was standing next to the first bus on the right side, with another two soldiers standing next to him. They were observing as we all went in. When we all went in, a soldier went in with an automatic rifle and stood next to the driver. Then General Mladic entered, he told the driver, "Close the door and follow the red car, just go after them." The red car was standing in front of the buses. The driver closed the door, the red car set off. Mladic stayed by the side of the road. He didn't go in the red car. We set off then. We asked the driver where are we going now? He said, well, you heard what he said. I don't know anything more. All I can do is follow the red car, wherever they go, I will go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a second. During the period of time that you were separated from your family up until the point that you were taken to the bus, did you have your belongings with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, were the belongings of the other people that were separated from their families taken away from them up until that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: No. They had their things with them, whoever had what with them, but nothing was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you said that the driver had indicated that he was to follow this red car. Tell us what happened on that bus trip and where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. The road went through Bratunac in the direction of Serbia, up to the Drina. When we came to Bratunac, he took a different road, turning towards Kravica. He didn't reach the bus station. A little bit before the Bratunac bus station, he turned right, through the town. Since it was night, I could see next to a building there was a school. We passed it. And then we stopped at a place. There were about 10 or 15 Serb soldiers waiting for us there. Then another bus opened its doors and they said, "Get out and go to the warehouse here." So we were leaving the bus and getting into this warehouse. It was an abandoned warehouse, not familiar to me before then. Us from both buses went inside this warehouse and sat down. We were surrounded by guards at the door. After a little while, vehicles would come again and people were entering the warehouse once more, until the warehouse was filled. When it was full, and it couldn't fit in any more people, nobody else came. Nobody else was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you went past a school. Can I ask you how do you know that it was a school that you had gone past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. Because it had large windows. Schools usually have a lot of windows. Other buildings have smaller and fewer windows. So that's how I know that it was a system of school -- a school system. And then someone came in front of the door and said, in a sharp voice, "12 of you should work according to the assignment that was given to you. Is that clear?" And the group said that it was clear to them. And again, there was silence. Then they came with torches and turned them on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you for a second and we'll get to this, but about how many people were brought to this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: The warehouse where I was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: At least 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And of those people, were they all elderly or infirm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. All elderly and/or infirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you brought when you first got off the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: When we went out there in Bratunac, to this warehouse where we were held for 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you describe what the interior of that building was like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: The building was white inside, painted white, but it was dirty. You couldn't really see much of the white. It was all scrawled over, the children had been scrawling all over the walls, the walls were crumbling. It seemed as if it was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it a brick building or was it made of some other material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: It was a brick building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you describe the floor of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: There was no floor, but they were just the planks where the floor used to be, and there was sand in between the planks, and that's what we were sitting on. As you entered, there was a glass two metres high. It was frosted glass, reinforced glass, and it was from two metres up all the way to the ceiling. There was nothing on the sides. There were no windows on the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you refer to a glass, as it reads in the record, are you talking about a window or are you talking about some other structure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: It was a window, it was just a large window, from one end to the other of that warehouse. It was like a window, but you were not able to open it. It was closed, it was large, and you could see that it was reinforced glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the interior of the space, was it an open space or was it divided into rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: In the morning, I saw that there was another smaller room. As for the large one, I don't know, I didn't see it. I saw that in the morning and there was a corridor and then to the left side there was a smaller room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you describe the entry to that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: The entrance to the building, I think, well, there was a kind of awning in front of the building. The door was large, although there was no door, and the entrance was in a straight line. There were no steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you learn at any time while you were there what that building was and where it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I found out later, but I didn't know it at the time, because some said it was a warehouse. I could see that for myself. It couldn't be anything else, but later I found out that such a warehouse was made in Kravica and that this one was abandoned and then all the cooperative things that were there were transferred to Kravica, to the Kravica warehouse, and that this one was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you find out at any point where this particular warehouse was in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: They told me later that it was behind the school, Vuk Karadzic. I couldn't really tell. They didn't tell me anything as to how many metres away, and I couldn't really estimate that from the bus or anything, how far it was from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were -- from whom did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I heard it in the warehouse. They said that this was a co-op warehouse. I didn't really ask any more. Then later in Tuzla I found out that it was a cooperative warehouse until a warehouse was built in Kravica, and then when it was built in Kravica, I asked, all right, so was this one abandoned and they said, yes, a warehouse was made in Kravica and then this one was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From the time that you were first brought to this location, about how long were you there while other people were being brought in? Until about what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: They were bringing people in until about midnight, until 12.00. They didn't have any more room there, and they didn't bring any more people in because the warehouse was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the conditions were like in the warehouse? Was any provision made for food and water and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Nothing. We were just suffocating in that warehouse. It was hot, and then the heat spread from one to another, and we were suffocating, and they didn't give us food or water. Only the next day in the morning did they start bringing water to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did -- did anybody complain about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. We did complain but they just fired over our heads and said, "Silence. I'm going to kill you all if I hear another word from you."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that the soldiers came in at some point with flashlights. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes. And then they asked who is from what village? They were asking about some villages around Bratunac. Some immediately responded and then they continued, are there any people from Glogova, actually they asked about Glogova first. Is there anyone here from Glogova? I don't know if two or three people responded, elderly men from Voljavica. Is there anyone from Hranca? And then people said, yes, they pointed the torches at them, and then they said, those who had torches pointed at them should get up and leave. Then that person would stand up and said, "Should I take a bag?" And then said, "No, no, you won't be needing anything anymore." Then when they went out they went to the left side, the same side that we entered. And this person was giving them a command, "Go there in front of them." He would go there, and then we would hear just blunt blows. Some people were moaning, screaming, when they were hit with something on their head. You wouldn't hear a word. And then we would hear something like, "All right, he's finished. Just drag him off over there." And then again, they would come with the torch, point it at people, pick who they wanted, they didn't ask anymore who you were or where you were from, just the people that had the torches pointed at them had to get at and go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that while this was going on that the soldiers were picking certain people, that there was any pattern to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: The next day we saw that they were picking those who looked a bit fitter than those who were completely infirm. There was already when it got light, so they were choosing people. But when they were just pointing the torches at people, you couldn't really tell who they were choosing. I think that they were actually choosing people who seemed to be more fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how many people did you see selected during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I didn't count, but in my estimate perhaps about 40 were taken out that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were any of the people that were taken out that night actually returned or brought back into the -- into this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: I will say later how many there were. When they beat somebody there and they were all bloodied, then they would point the torch at them and say, "Look how they are." Two would be taking him under the arm pits and then they would just shove that person at us, and then they would command that they be dragged at the sides of the warehouse. So that happened from time to time. In the morning when it got light, then we found out that out of those people who had been beaten, five had died. They took out five people out of those who had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And overnight, did you hear any shooting at all that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: There was just one shot. They shot Hamed Efendic. There were no more shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you see Hamed Efendic actually taken out of the building at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was -- that's what the people who were next to him. Him and Ibran Mustic [as interpreted] were brought in by car. The two of them came in by themselves, and the people who were next to them asked them how did you get here? And they said we were brought here by car. And then Ibran Mustafic was taken out first. There was some kind of shouting, a sort of quarrel amongst them, and then Ibran did not come back any more. Then they called Hamed Efendic. Hamed went out. You couldn't hear anything of what happened there. All you could hear was a shot, actually four bullets maybe. And then they said, "You can drag him away. He's finished. He's dead. Drag him off." You didn't hear any more shots, anymore. You could just hear blunt blows on those people who had been taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, of the five people that you indicated that had died and were taken out in the morning, I should say rather after that, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: In the morning? In the morning, when it got light, they were complaining that they couldn't hold these people any more in their laps. They wanted them to be taken out. Then they permitted that these people could be taken out, then they dragged them by the arms or the legs. They dragged them out. And I could see them taking out five dead people. Then when those people came back, they were crying, we asked them what's going on? What's happen being outside? They said, you should see the pile of dead who are here behind the warehouse. It's a horror. And they were just there crying. They sat down. Then we were allowed -- well, you could hear some kind of machinery coming there, buses, trucks. Then one of the soldiers came and he said, "I need ten people. I need them to do something." We didn't know what this was about. But they -- we -- the others had told us what's going on outside so nobody wanted to go outside but it already got light, so they chose you, you, you, about ten people who were supposed to go out. And it was quiet for about an hour or so. And then again you could hear those trucks leaving the warehouse. And those ten either never came back to be with us in the warehouse again. We don't know what happened to them. Then again, they started to take people out and kill them. Then we were allowed to use a room that was just next to the warehouse to use it as a toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say again they started to take people out and kill them, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, we would know because one of them would come and say, "You, get up." And then when he'd get up and leave, then you could hear a blow and then a fall. We could hear all of that. We knew that that person had been killed and then the next one would be taken. When they let us go to that toilet, then they would take someone by the shoulder and then that person would be taken to the left and they would say, you go here, and who would not be taken by the shoulder, then that person would go to that room that was used as a toilet. My turn also came to go and when I was getting out then one man was taken by the shoulder. And I was watching from this room how three or four of them were on one side and three or four on the other side, and this person -- this other person was watching him holding an automatic rifle, and then this person holding an automatic rifle would say come to me, come to me, and then he would start moving towards him, between the others, and then the one from the left-hand side hit him with an iron bar on the head, and on his back, and he fell. The first soldier on the right-hand side had an axe and hit him on the backbone with an axe, and he fell while this man was still holding the axe. I saw his legs and feet, but I didn't hear any screams or anything like that. I went back to the warehouse after that. This went on until the afternoon. In the afternoon, again, we heard trucks coming, two trucks came, the same procedure, again they asked for ten and then ten would be assigned, who would go to do something, and then they would be separated and they would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, about how many people in your estimation were killed from that morning, the day light, from daylight, until that afternoon? And just so the record is clear, we are talking about the morning of the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Well, around 40 were killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how many in your estimation were killed over night, that is from the time that you arrive until the time you arrived on the 12th, until daylight on 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Oh, you mean during the night only? Until dawn? Is that what you're asking me or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Oh, during the night, around 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, that afternoon, tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: Then these vehicles arrived again, two of them, again they selected ten people to go and do something for them. That's what they said. Again, there was some quiet for about an hour while these vehicles were leaving the warehouse, both vehicles left. Those ten never returned to our warehouse either, those ten who got out then. Then there was a bit of quiet, nothing was going on then. Then we asked these soldiers what they are -- these guards what they are going to do with us? And they said, "We don't know. We don't know what's going to happen to you tonight." And then one of them said, now you've got Mladic coming and you can ask him what's going to happen to you and where you'll be going. Mladic appeared on the -- at the door, between these two guards, and then all of us said in a single voice, why are you torturing us here? Why are you not taking us away if you said you would? He said well an agreement could not have been reached until now, if an agreement was possible with you, this wouldn't have happened in the first place. Now you're being taken to Kalesija for an exchange. But one should get up and count you so that I could give you all transportation. One man got up and counted us and said there is 296 of us. And he said, all right, wait a bit now, you're going to have transportation now, and then you're going to move on. He left, we heard vehicles arriving there, and then they said to us, "Come on, get up. The buses are there. One by one in a column to the buses." So I got up too and when I got out, it was still day-time, it wasn't dark yet. I saw a Boksit Milici and a Centrotrans Sarajevo bus. As for the rest I didn't even look what kind of buses they were. I entered the Centrotrans Sarajevo bus. That's how we all boarded. When I got into the bus, to the left of the bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just finish your sentence and I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: All right. Say about ten metres away from the bus, there was General Mladic standing there and about ten soldiers standing in front of him, and he was showing his hand this way and saying something to them. Then when it got dark, we set out. Again, one Serb soldier would enter the bus and stand next to the driver. The soldier had an automatic rifle. And we said, "Where are we being taken now?" And he said, "Well, most probably you're being taken to Kalesija to an exchange as he told you," and he said, "What did Maddic say to you?" And we said what it was, and then he said well then most probably you are being taken for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From the time that you arrived at that building until the time that you left, that is as a group, did you -- were you allowed to keep your property, your things that were brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-169
utterances.text: See, I always forget to say something. In the morning, when all of these people were taken away, when everything was over, then one man came to the door, and well he was tall with dark hair, short dark hair, also wearing a camouflage uniform, he said, "Now all of your things, your IDs, wallets, watches, hand in all of that." And then we were giving all of this to the people who were the next to us, and he was just throwing all of this into a bag, and then he said money, money, too.
